items.title: The Atrocities That Shaped the Modern Middle East
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of the seemingly forgotten attack on the Yazidi people by ISIS in 2014. Then, David is joined by the historian Simon Sebag Montefiore to discuss his new book, The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East . David and Simon discuss how much of the present-day Middle East emerged from the ruins of the Ottoman empire and the violence that took place both before and after the empire’s collapse. David and Simon discuss how, one after another, different language groups and religious groups were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether. Then, David finishes with a discussion of The Hidden Hand : The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda, by Warren Kinsella. The following is a transcript of the episode: Simon Sebag Montefiore: So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing, and if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression. David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Simon Sebag Montefiore, the acclaimed British historian and author of the new book The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East . The book discussion at the end of the show will feature The Hidden Hand by Warren Kinsella, subtitled The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda. But before either the dialogue with Simon Sebag Montefiore or the book discussion of The Hidden Hand , some opening thoughts on themes that will run all their way through today’s program. Simon Sebag’s book The Cauldron describes the transformation of the Middle East from its existence under the Ottoman empire a century and a half ago to the region of today, divided among many nations. And yet while the map of the Middle East is much more tangled than it was when the Ottomans ruled almost everything from Tunisia to Iraq—although parts of it were under foreign influence: British and French colonial rule, Italian colonial rule—a simple map, but with a complex reality. Simon Sebag describes how, one after another, different language groups, different religious groups, different groups with different histories were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether. I want to showcase just one of those acts of elimination to drive home what it is that we are talking about when we talk about the making of the modern Middle East. In August 2014, fighters of the Islamic terror group ISIS attacked the Yazidi minority in northwest Iraq. The Yazidis are a very ancient people who follow a pre-Islamic religion. There are about 600,000 of them living in northwest Iraq in August 2014. ISIS murdered some 3,000 to 5,000 of them , mostly men and older women, and captured 6,800 women and girls and turned them into sexual slaves for ISIS fighters, and spared the lives of some of the very young boys in order to recruit them and brainwash them as child soldiers fighting for ISIS. Religious and cultural sites belonging to the Yazidi people were systematically destroyed, and civilian infrastructure, especially water supplies, wrecked. Four hundred thousand of the 600,000 Yazidi were driven into exile, and few of those people have ever returned to their homes. Now, this was a true genocide. ISIS was very explicit. Their goal was to eliminate the Yazidi people, because ISIS hated their religious traditions. ISIS condemned the non-Islamic Yazidi as devil worshipers and thought that because of their non-Islamic views, they should cease to exist as a people and even as human beings. The story was a temporary big deal. People in the West were aware of the Yazidi genocide, and some of the Yazidi were given refuge, especially in Europe. But as time has passed, the story has faded from memory. It is no longer of much interest. You certainly don’t see the kind of big marches in Western countries by progressive people or other kinds of people that you’ve seen in, for example, the war that Hamas started in October of 2023. The Yazidi story doesn’t seem to matter. And I think the reason why we have a hard time holding onto it is because a lot of people who study the Middle East, especially the progressive-minded, have a kind of vision of how the Middle East should be. It’s a vision in which Arab nationalism and Islamic identity are seen as progressive, in the most literal sense—the trend of the future—and everything else is seen as kind of backward looking, and it shouldn’t be there. And so as Christian populations were either eliminated by force or driven into exile—as Simon and I will discuss, there were massacres of the Assyrian Christian population in Iraq. Much of the Christian population of Egypt has been driven into exile. The Armenians were the victim of two waves of genocide in Ottoman empire, one in the 1890s and again in the 1910s. The Kurds were subjected to murderous attack by Saddam Hussein’s Iraq and by the Iranian regime, too. And of course, there is the story of the Jews, who inhabited ancient communities in places like Alexandria and Baghdad, communities that existed before the coming of either the Arabs or of Islam to the region. And after 1945, those communities—or after 1941 in the Iraqi case—those communities were murdered, massacred, plundered, driven into exile, ceased to exist, in-gathered into the state of Israel, where the Jews who formerly lived all through the Ottoman empire have found refuge in one place. This great system of simplification was at every turn marked by atrocity, attempted genocide, the refusal of difference within the context of the Middle East. We don’t seem to find that so troubling because we have an implicit idea of who should be on top and who should not be on top. And this implicit understanding may, I think, add some context to why false accusations against Israel and the Jews have gained so much hearing. Because in a way, the Jews and the state of Israel stand out as the great exception to the trend of the Middle East. This is the one place—the one place—where a people that were a minority people under the old Ottoman empire have built a successful state that is able to be self-sufficient. And that exception to the trend everywhere else in the Middle East is seen by many as a kind of denial of the logic of history, which calls for the whole region to become all one thing under one language—or two, Turkish and Arabic—under one faith, Islam, everyone else driven to the wall. We’re going to talk a little bit about this in the program, how this happened, and we’re going to try to talk about it from an historical point of view to understand it. It is, I think, a trend to be condemned, but first, before condemning, it is a trend to be understood. And to understand why the state of Israel looms so large in our imagination, we have to pay some attention to the things that loom strangely small, like the story of the Yazidi. So horrible, so forgotten. Why? And now, my dialogue with Simon Sebag Montefiore. [ Music ] Frum: Simon Sebag Montefiore is a British historian of Russia and the Middle East whose books have been published in more than 40 languages. His nonfiction—he has written fiction too—his nonfiction includes: Catherine the Great and Potemkin ; Stalin: The Court of the Red Tsar ; and also Young Stalin , as well as the internationally best-selling Jerusalem and the history of The Romanovs: 1613–1918 . He received his Ph.D. from Cambridge and is a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. He lives in London. His new book is The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East, a history of the region from the last years of the Ottoman Sultanate to the present day. Simon, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. Simon Sebag Montefiore: Lovely to be with you, David. Frum: So first, congratulations on the astonishing acclaim for The Cauldron. And thank you for making time in what has been obviously an exhausting media tour. You’ve been everywhere, so I’m so honored you would join. Montefiore: Thank you. And thanks for having me on this. I’ve always wanted to do this, so here we are finally. Frum: The Cauldron is this thrilling narrative history of the Middle East from approximately the year 1900 under the Ottoman empire to the present day, with characters that are presented very vividly: many anecdotes, many quotations from the literature of the region. The book is a tremendous linguistic achievement. And it’s an exciting read, but it’s also one that can be read not necessarily from beginning to end, but you can start from the middle and work outwards if you prefer, because it’s addressed regionally. But I want to test a thesis on you. So this is a narrative history. It’s a story, and a thrilling story. But you’re not an argumentative historian. Your own ideas are sort of present in the background but are not in the foreground. I want to try to assess what I think you’re telling us. Let me lay out what I think is your thesis, and then you can tell me whether I have it right or whether I have it wrong. May I go ahead? Montefiore: Please do. Frum: Okay. So if we start in the year 1900—let’s start a little before. Let’s start 10 years before that. Most of what is now the Middle East is ruled by the Ottoman empire. So what is now Turkey, parts of Southern Europe, what is now Iraq, what is now Syria, what is now Lebanon, what is now Israel and the West Bank. Egypt is theoretically part of the Ottoman empire, although not practically. Tunisia is theoretically part of the Ottoman empire, not practically. Libya too. And across this vast array of space, there are dominant groups, especially the Ottoman Turkish-speaking Sunni Muslims, but there are many, many minority groups in many, many cities. And it’s not an egalitarian society, it’s not a just society, and it’s not a progressive society. It’s kind of backward-looking. But still, if you’re a Greek in Smyrna, if you’re a Greek in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, if you are an Armenian in one of the cities of the empire, if you’re a Jew in Baghdad, if you’re a Yazidi peasant, an Assyrian Christian—there’s a way forward for you, both as a people and for you as individuals. And suddenly that begins to change—and you’ll know why I’m dating this back to 1890 rather than 1900—with a process that unfolds over the next decades, of brutal simplification. That’s the cauldron: the great melting. Brutal simplification. Minorities are massacred or driven into exile, and the two big dominant groups—Turkish-speaking people and Arabic-speaking people—assert greater and greater control and intolerance over the region, driving everyone else out. And that is what the cauldron is. So do I have it right? Montefiore: That’s one part of it. One part of it is an increasingly tightening nationalistic control that does ultimately lead to what is in fact the biggest kind of slow, ethnic-cleansing purge over the last 125 years, which is the destruction of and the vanishing of the Christians of the Middle East. And that is one of the parts of what you’re referring to here. One is a sort of tightening of a nationalistic control. And the other one is a driving out of anyone who doesn’t fit into that. And the Christian population—it’s such an extraordinary thing. You know, in 630 A.D., the Middle East was basically sort of 90 percent Christian, just before the Arab conquests. And then over the next sort of thousand years, 25 percent remained Christian. And so in 1900, the time you’re talking about, or 1890, you know, still 25 percent of the Middle East is Christian. And jump ahead to today, and that population has virtually vanished. It’s something like 4 percent now. Frum: Well, let’s start with one of those populations, which underwent a brutal process of murder. This is not an abstract historical process. And I’m speaking, of course, of the Armenians—and that’s why I backdated to 1890, not 1900, because the attacks on Armenians begin in the 1890s. Tell us the story of the Armenians within the Ottoman empire, and why they are so brutally treated. Montefiore: The Armenians had lived since time immemorial, since ancient times, in this region. They didn’t have a single homeland. They were spread across the Ottoman empire. But before the Ottoman empire, in the early modern period or the Middle Ages, there had been Armenian kingdoms in Eastern Anatolia. And of course, in ancient times, there had been full Armenian kingdoms in that region, and Armenian kingdoms had been buffer zones between the Persian or Parthian and the Roman Empires. They had been among the first people to convert from paganism to Christianity, and they never converted to Islam. And in the Ottoman empire, they remained a powerful community, a self-governing community that was recognized as Christian, provided they paid, like all other non-Muslim communities, the jizya —that’s the tax for people of the book. And their community was, like the Greek community, which was another large community within the Ottoman empire, also recognized. But there were spasms of violence against them whenever economics or war or famine, or there was a crisis in which one would blame the other within one’s community. But jump forward to the late 19th century. For many centuries—you put this very well in your introduction, David—but for many centuries, these minorities had been allowed to govern themselves, but they didn’t have equal rights to the ruling Ottoman Turkish Sunni Muslims. But that changed beginning in the 1830s and intensifying in the 1850s with Tanzimat. That made all Ottoman citizens equal, whether they were Christian, Greek, Armenian, Jewish. Frum: Tanzimat means “reform.” Is that right? Montefiore: It means reform. And the idea of reform was not necessarily to turn the Ottoman empire into a liberal democracy, but to make it more powerful, to exploit its peoples, to make the empire stronger. But in fact, what it did, in part, was, in part it liberated these minorities and enabled them to own land, to expand their businesses, to become wealthy. And many dynasties emerged in trade and so on that were Armenian and Greek overwhelmingly. And that caused immense jealousy amongst the Muslim population that had been the ruling class for all this time, or the ruling caste for all these centuries. And it also discombobulated the empire. And this policy only went on for about 20 years. In 1877, 1879, a new sultan attacked by Russia, fighting for the existence of his dynasty and his empire, came back. Abolished the new parliament that had been part of these Tanzimat or the climax of these Tanzimat reforms, and unleashed a new idea of Islamic empire, Islamic Ottomanism, in which the senior peoples were now the Muslims. And the sultan rebranded himself as sultan caliph of the empire. And at that point— Frum: Sultan means “power holder”; caliph means “religious leader.” Montefiore: Yeah. It meant the sort of successor to the prophet. And at this point, Abdul Hamid II, a fascinating character, started to promote a new concept in the empire where he played off different minorities against other minorities to promote essentially the Islamic nature of the state or the empire. And this involved using, for example, Kurds, who were sort of second-class Muslim citizens, to attack Armenians, who were third-class Ottoman citizens in effect. And this unleashed all sorts of notorious massacres. The Bulgarian massacres—they were also known as the Hamidian massacres after Hamid himself, the sultan. And at the same time, something else was happening. Which was the excuse for this, which was that nationalism had arrived amongst these peoples. And just as the Turks started to embrace nationalism, the Arabs started to embrace it, and the Serbs and all the Christian peoples of Europe started to embrace it, so did the Armenians. And some Armenians now started to say, like: We want a state too. Everyone else has one. Where can we have one? And they naturally found a backer in the Ottoman empire’s main enemy—which was the Russian Empire, which was the Orthodox Christian empire of the Romanovs. And so now when they looked at the Ottomans, they started to think, Not only are these people Christian Ottomans, they’re actually Christian Russian agents who are holding a dagger right at the heart of the Ottoman empire. And it was made worse because, though the Armenians were mainly concentrated in the eastern part of what is now Turkey, they actually were speckled around the whole empire. There were Armenians in Jerusalem. There were Armenians in Constantinople, the capital, and all over the empire. And therefore, they began to see them very like how Germans began to see Jews between the wars. And there hangs a tale, of course. So by the time we reach World War I—I’m jumping ahead here a bit, if I’m allowed—by the time we reach World War I and the Ottoman empire enters the war against the Allies on the side of Germany, of course Russia is on the side of the Allies and against the Ottoman empire and is, of course, backing the Armenians. And the Ottoman regime at this point has changed from the Ottomanism autocracy of Abdul Hamid II to the ultra neo-fascist, almost proto-Nazi eugenist nationalism of the Young Turks. Who were led by the three Pashas, who were the kind of triumvirate that ruled the Ottoman empire during the war, and they believed that war would be a cleansing experience for the Ottoman empire. Frum: And they attacked the Armenian communities. In the 1890s, there were Ottoman riots against Armenians in the cities. And during the war, there’s a murderous rampage against the Armenians who are not in the cities. What is the total death toll among Armenians between 1895 and 1918? Montefiore: It’s about 2 million. Frum: About 2 million. Montefiore: I mean, during World War I, 1.1 million is the usually accepted number, which is colossal. And it’s a large part of the Armenian nation. And it’s such a decisive moment because it’s because of this genocide—and by the way, this wasn’t the only genocide. They also killed 300,000 Maronite Christians in Lebanon. They also killed over 400,000 Greeks or Pontic Greeks who were on the Black Sea coast and in Ionia. They also killed several hundred thousand Assyrian Christians who lived on the borders of what is now Turkey and Iraq. And so this was a deliberate purge. And there is evidence, there are directives, there are orders from Talat Pasha and the other leaders to either massacre these people, men, women, and children, or to drive them out into the desert to starve. And it’s really the first modern genocide. Frum: And it’s a modern genocide unlike what Stalin will do to his subject peoples, where he’s trying to break economic resistance. This is ethnic elimination by—it’s maybe not a fully modern state, the Ottoman state. It’s obviously not as efficient as Germany and not as efficient as Stalin’s Russia. But it is the deliberate elimination of categories of ethnicity in order to simplify the state, to make the state more powerful. Montefiore: That’s right. And also to destroy the bacteria within, to destroy the traitors within. And so it’s decisive in various ways. One is that it ensures that the Armenian nation exists really more in diaspora than it does in formerly Armenian territories. It led the Western powers to back Armenian nationhood as well. And Armenian forces fought on the side of the Russians in the wars that followed. And in the wars that followed the fall of the Ottoman empire, they fought against the new Turkish state to try and win an Armenian state, which was designated to exist in what is now eastern Turkey. And its big backer was President Woodrow Wilson of America, who promised to rule, to govern a mandate—an American mandate—for the Armenians, which is quite a thought. Of course, this never happened. And in fact, what happened was, as David will know better than I, Wilson went back to America and failed to get any of these obligations through Congress or membership of the League of Nations that he’d created and so on. But what happened in the former Ottoman empire was that a new Turkish-nationalist maestro arose: Mustafa Kemal Pasha, who became [Mustafa Kemal] Atatürk. The master of the father of Turks, who founded a new Turkish nation, who founded a Turkish republic, and crushed the Armenians in eastern Turkey. So they never got the republic. Frum: And then drove out the Greeks from western Turkey. Montefiore: And then switched round and drove out the Greeks from western Turkey, and that’s also a fascinating part of the story. Frum: I’m going to pause you there, because there’s an element here that is going to, I think, come as a pause or something to a lot of modern readers. If you have studied Middle Eastern studies at an American university, or even more a European or British university, you’re introduced to the Middle East as a kind of inert mass. Nothing happens there unless a Western power makes it happen, and anything that happens there is a reaction to something that a Western power does. But as you were telling it, the beginning of the cycle of purging, elimination, ethnic cleansing, genocide—it’s a spontaneous local phenomenon. This is something driven by the Ottoman Turkish government and their successor, the Young Turk government, which is defining itself in new ways against its subject peoples in an effort to exert stronger control over its territory. Montefiore: That’s right. Frum: It’s not a reaction to Western neocolonialism or Western imperialism. This is something they wanted to do for their own reasons and acted on their own volition. Montefiore: Yeah. This is Ottoman Turkish imperialism. This is Ottoman Turkish genocidal massacre of their own subjects for their own purposes. And it’s a sort of proto-Nazi ideology with social Darwinism, eugenicism, and ultranationalism, and this comes from within the Middle East itself. Though, of course, they’re highly influenced, as are all the peoples of the region, by nationalism—the new drug of nationalism that seems to offer the solution to all things. Frum: Let me hit another pause button here because—and I wanted to pause before we got to Atatürk, because the First World War ends with the collapse of the Ottoman empire. It’s carved up. It loses most of its remaining European territories, and many of its holdings are then divided up into new Arab countries that either have outright Sunni majorities or else have Sunni elites, as is the case in Iraq. Most people in Iraq are not Sunni, but there’s an Arab Sunni elite, and there are then other groups. And what we now call Turkey is also a successor state. It’s carved out of the Ottoman empire, too, and it’s defined as a national state with Turkish as its language. It changes the name of its capital city from the Greek Constantinople to the kind-of-Greek Istanbul—which is also Greek, I understand, but it sounds more Turkish even though it’s Greek in origin. So we have these now-new states. And the Arab states and the new Turkish national state, they begin eliminating their minorities one by one by one. Montefiore: That’s correct. And so, you know, in Turkey, for example what happens, the new Turkish state is really defined on what we would now call, in progressive parlance, an ethno-religious basis. In the sense that Turks were Ottoman subjects who spoke Turkish, lived in what was regarded as the Turkish heartland, and were Muslim. And people who were Christian could not be Turkish. So what we see today—and it started with Atatürk’s version of Turkishness, but his was secular and this is religious. So that’s exactly right. And so they drove out the Armenians who had challenged them and tried to carve out a state in the east, and then they turned on the Greeks. And the Greeks—it was slightly a different story, because the Greeks had been promised a sort of new Byzantine Empire in what is now western Turkey. And the reason why they claimed that was because there were huge Greek Orthodox populations in western Turkey—that used to be called Ionia—that had been there for thousands of years, literally since the Trojan Wars. And they lived in cities like Smyrna, the great Greek city of Smyrna. And so now Greek armies arrived, backed by the British and the French—and this was an example of European interference in the region—they arrived to protect their own ancient local Greek populations, but also to increase their kingdom. The Greek kingdom, the Greek state. And there they encountered Atatürk and his new Turkish army. And what ensued was a brutal nation-building war of ethnic purging, population swaps. Brutal, huge battles of regular armies. The armies in this were huge. They were 150,000 strong each in these major battles, with artillery, of course, and everything. So they were real World War I battles. But this is in 1922, and the Turks won these battles, and they then drove out, massacring and driving and deporting the Greek populations of what is now western Turkey. And in 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne, which involved Britain and Greece, the populations were swapped. So all the Muslims went to Turkey, all the Christians were expelled— Frum: That sounds so antiseptic. Montefiore: It’s not that antiseptic, because there were huge massacres. Frum: It’s murder, it’s pillage, it’s people standing on docks. It’s cities on fire. Montefiore: Yeah. It’s people jumping into docks and drowning. It’s burning cities. And at the heart of it is the inferno of Smyrna, which is one of the most apocalyptic urban demolitions of all time. And this creation of the Turkish nation is so important, because it explains what we’re seeing now in the rise of Turkey as a regional power. And it explains both the militaristic Turkish nationalism. It explains also the aspiration for much more influence, the grievance that they were diminished inside these borders agreed on in 1923, and the wish to expand and re-energize the Ottoman idea. And that is what we’re seeing now with President [Recep Tayyip] Erdogan. Frum: Let me take you now to the Arabic-speaking countries, mostly Sunni, that are carved out of the Ottoman empire. Now, Egypt was notionally part of the Ottoman empire in the 19th century. It was really an independent state with a lot of British influence, some French influence. Egypt remains a reasonably cosmopolitan place after the First World War with Greek minorities, Jewish minorities. Syria has more French influence. Lebanon has a lot of French influence. Palestine, which is reserved as a Jewish homeland, is a British mandate. But there’s this new country of Iraq created, and it becomes kind of genocide central in the Arabic-speaking Middle East. Tell us about the history of Iraq from the end of the First World War to the advent of the Second World War. Montefiore: Well, that’s right. But the Egypt you described was—and it’s hard to imagine now—but Egypt was the most cosmopolitan country in the Middle East. The fellahin, the lower, you know, the peasant class, were Arab, but the merchant classes were—as you said, David—Jewish, Lebanese, Greek, Italian. And they were large populations. The Jewish population was several hundred thousand just on its own, and they were the descendants of Jews who had been settled in Egypt by Alexander the Great and the Ptolemies, so they’d been there for millennia. And the wealth of Egypt depended on this mercantile class. And then the ruling class, the landowners, were Turco-Circassians, who were the descendants of enslaved Christians who had been enslaved and kidnapped by the Ottomans and previous rulers from their villages. They were Christian children who’d been enlisted in the Ottoman or Mamluk armies, who had been stolen from their parents, who were probably murdered. And who had then been converted to Islam, manumitted, and then joined the army and founded these families, these dynasties. It’s just a fascinating story. And even in the 1920s, these people, the Turco-Circassians, were still owning and ruling Egypt. And the ruling kings of Egypt, as they became, were also Turco-Albanian dynasty, who didn’t even speak Arabic right into the 1930s, which is fascinating. So that’s Egypt. And so you’re absolutely right that these are incredibly complicated because of Ottoman countries. When you come to Syria and Lebanon, these are also multiethnic, multi-sectarian countries—as they still are, which is why their rulers to this day are desperately struggling to make them work as single countries. And the French mandate was for Greater Syria, which is now divided into Syria and Lebanon. But it’s just worth remembering how different these countries could have been. Because when one thinks of them as they were bound to be Syria and Lebanon, no, that isn’t how it worked at all. And that’s also true with Iraq. With Syria and Lebanon, the French were thinking about dividing it into five or six countries. And those countries were two Sunni ones in Aleppo and Damascus, and then a Druze one, an Alawite one at Latakia on the coast. And then they were going to devise a Christian Maronite country that the Christians would rule, who were the French allies in Lebanon. And in the end, they decided not to do this, but to divide it into two big countries: Syria and Lebanon. So then we get to Iraq. Again, one thinks of Iraq as set, but Iraq was known to the allies as Mesopotamia—“the land between the rivers” in Greek. Iraq was an old Arab name for this region, but there’d never been a country called Iraq before, just as there’d never been a country called Lebanon or Syria or Jordan. And these countries were all drawn by the Western overlords, particularly Britain and France. And Iraq was just a combination of three provinces, or vilayets, put together by the British. And the vilayets were Basra, Baghdad, and Mosul. And Mosul is where the oil was, and that’s the Kurdish area. And there was a big question as to whether Mosul would be in Iraq or not. And that’s a pretty important detail, because it’s partly the Kurdish area; it’s where the oil is. And the Turks, who we were just discussing a minute ago, wanted Mosul and believed Mosul should be in Turkey. Now, that would have really changed the situation. But the Western allies also wanted to create a state—not just for the Armenians that we were discussing, but for the Kurds. And the Kurds would have a state that was partly in what is now Turkey and partly in what is now Iraq. But that didn’t happen either, because the Kurds were betrayed by everybody. And talk about genocide; this is another genocide in the 1930s where Atatürk and the Turkish Republic bombed Kurdish revolts, destroyed Kurdish village, killed something like 40,000 to 50,000 using poison gas, bombing villages. And they crushed the Kurds for another generation. In Iraq, they hoped to get Mosul or at least to prevent a Kurdish state being created. And in the end, the British were determined that Mosul would stay in the new country they’d created of Iraq. But as you said, David, Iraq was a multiethnic, multinational, multi-sectarian country. It had a small Shia majority, a barely Sunni minority. But that minority was very educated—was the landowners, was the civil servants. And it had been favored and empowered by the Turks, who were also Sunni. And then there were huge minorities of Kurds, small Christian sects, the Chaldeans, and Assyrians. And when I say “small,” they were a million people, so they weren’t that tiny. Non-Muslim sects like the Yazidis and Turkmen and all sorts of other minorities. Assyrians who were Christian. Frum: And Jews in Baghdad. Montefiore: And Jews in Baghdad. And a third of Baghdad was Jewish. Yeah. And many of the great families there like the Sassoons, most famously, who later went to England and became the sort of richest family in England, basically. The Sassoons, “the Rothschilds of the East,” they were known as. They were an incredibly prosperous minority, and they dominated the city in many ways. And the most kind of privileged of them ran huge business empires and also served the Pashas who ran Baghdad and— Frum: And between 1919 and 1942, there’s just attack after attack on each of these groups: on the Assyrian Christians, on the Kurds, on the Jews. And they are murdered and driven into exile. Montefiore: That’s exactly what happened. One of the big outrages is in the early ’30s, when they turn on the Christian Assyrians and massacre them. The Assyrians flee the country. And it’s really the first sign in Iraq that these new nation-states created for the Arabs are actually contradicting the multiethnic kind of cosmopolitan nature of these regions, that had been, perhaps in some ways, at various moments—and one mustn’t generalize—better ruled by empires with capitals far away. And so the climax for the Jews comes in 1941 with the Farhud, which is a terrifying pogrom. But in these pogroms against the Jews in 1941, influenced by specifically Nazi propaganda and perpetrated by a self-consciously Nazi-influenced militia, it was an episode more like October the 7, you know—where women were raped and then their bodies mutilated. Body parts were paraded through the town. And it really took place at an interesting moment when the British were about to retake Baghdad, and a pro-Nazi government was just in the process of being overthrown in 1941. And in that interim period, they decided they were going to get the Jews, and they went round the town marking the doors of every Jewish house. And so when the Farhud started, when the pogrom started, they knew exactly the houses, and they could see the mark on the door. Which is just a sort of chilling detail, isn’t it, David? David Frum: Yeah. I want to bring now the story up to the present in our last few minutes. One of the things I think that you will hear said a lot on modern university campuses by advocacy groups of various kinds is—they’ll tell the story of this Edenic Middle East before the Jews got there, before the Jews came to the state of Israel. And they will ask, Why aren’t the Jews comfortable to live in a multiethnic, multinational state with an Arab majority? What could possibly go wrong in such a situation? And I wanted to give people a tour of that. The story of the Middle East from the weakening of the Ottoman empire, as you say, in the late 19th century, beginning with the attacks on the Armenians, most bloodily in the 1890s and continuing, is: You either have a state, or you’re dead. Those are your choices in the Middle East. Montefiore: That’s right, and that is one of the themes of the book. And one of the themes of the book is to confront all of these Edenic myths, which even a cursory look at the facts and the history will show you is entirely legendary and has never existed. You know, it starts with the myth that the Ottoman empire was this kind of wonderful kumbaya, tolerant, poetry-spouting kind of a multicultural society. And that was never true. It was a conquest society built on the enslavement and kidnapping of Christian children. This isn’t some sort of story, by the way. This is how the Ottoman empire, it was how it was so successful. This tribute of children—which the Ottoman empire took from Christian villages in the Caucasus, in the Crimea, in southern Ukraine, and also in the Balkans—was how it was provided with talented, energetic manpower. And the women went into the harems. The boys went into the army or the civil service. And the women in the harems. The most lucky of them became queens. They became the wives of actual sultans. And Hürrem Sultan, known as Roxelana, for example, the blonde or red-haired Ukrainian girl—who incidentally was the most powerful Ukrainian in world history, I would argue—she became Suleiman the Magnificent’s wife, mother of his successor. And she was typical, but of the luckiest of those. But for the boys, they became soldiers. They were forcefully converted to Islam. Once they were about to become officers, they were manumitted—in other words, freed from slavery—and then they were able to work up the military. And they were the army of the Ottoman empire that conquered this vast empire from the borders of Libya all the way to the borders of Iran. So that’s the first thing about the Ottoman empire. The second thing is: There was tolerance, provided you accepted the total supremacy of Islam and Sultan. And if you in any way challenged that political and religious supremacy, you were slaughtered. The history of the Ottoman empire is filled with massacres of minorities and Jews at regular intervals. And this goes on right into the 19th century, well before we get to the 1890s, where David started this discussion. But, you know, a typical example is in 1860; 25,000 Christians were massacred in Damascus in the 1860 event, which was one of the occurrences that brought the Western powers into the Ottoman empire. And we’ve seen how the Ottoman Empire ended, with a proto-Nazi genocide of entire races. And then you get into the creation of these states. If we look into the second half of the 20th century—where Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon, they all became independent—again, you see a similar pattern. Dictators from one sect or another protected and promoted their own group. Saddam Hussein, for example, protected the Sunni majority, even though he was from a very poor Tikriti peasant family, and brutally crushed the Shiites and the Kurds. And ultimately, to come back to your theme, this culminated in the attempted genocide of the Kurdish nation in Iraq. So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing. And if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression. And that is the process by which, in my book, you’ll see over a century and a quarter we go from this wonderful efflorescence of sects and ethnicities. You go to this bleaker and bleaker and bleaker environment, and the Christians virtually vanish. So that in 2000, like 25 years ago, you still had a million Christians in Iraq. After the Islamist insurgency during the Iraq War, now there are 115,000 Christians in Iraq. So 900,000 of them have gone. So this is the picture. Frum: And this process of consolidation also leads to economic and technological failure. So Egypt—the cosmopolitan Egypt you describe of the 19th century—there was a large stock market in Alexandria. Egypt was a food exporter. Cotton exporter. Montefiore: Huge cotton industry. Frum: A big, big destination for foreign investment. The Suez Canal. And then after the Second World War, Egypt, a newly nationalist, newly Arabized Egypt, expels its Greeks, Italians, Jews, of course. And imposes state control over the economy and becomes an ever-more poverty-stricken country, dependent evermore not on investment, but on aid. Montefiore: That’s right. Frum: That’s the story of every region. And this story is told as one that the West did to the Middle East, not as a story something the Middle East did to itself Montefiore: Agree. That is one of the major themes of the book. And you do have to question whether the nation-state itself was—as an ideology, as a state architecture—suited to this region at all. Frum: Well, let’s talk about one particular nation-state, which is the one that gets almost all the airtime, and that is the nation-state of Israel. Built over a century of gradual development, created by a vote of the United Nations in 1947. In 1947, there is a war of independence. The Arab population is pushed out of what will become Israel, or chooses to leave. In some cases leaves voluntarily. And then Jewish populations all over the rest of the Middle East are expelled in hundreds of thousands, and come to Israel. And a nation-state is built there that is actually economically capable, technologically capable, militarily capable. And this becomes the last and most intolerable provocation, that there is one nation-state that actually is suited to the region when other nation-states don’t work. Montefiore: That’s right. And also, I mean, there are other ways to look at Israel. I mean, one way to look at it—I look at the creation of Israel as very much just one of the states created out of the breakup of the Ottoman Empire, and out of the end of the British Empire too. But you know—the real comparison is, it’s very like the creation of Turkey, which is only 20 years earlier. Where you have a new concept of a new nation created with ethnic and religious characteristics, a newly defined language, and a brutal ethnic war. A competition with another people who are also indigenous to the region, in which many of them are expelled. Frum: This is Turks versus Greeks, compared to Jews versus Arabs. Montefiore: Yeah. And it’s very similar. Out of it comes a nation that is extremely proud, extremely competent, extremely dynamic, militaristic to some extent. And there are huge population swaps to make all this work. And out of it comes Turkey. Though Turkey remains with a massive ethnic population that doesn’t want to be in Turkey—the Kurds—and that leads to something like 100,000 civilians being killed over the next century. So does it sound like anywhere? Frum: Yeah. Well, you don’t have the Kingdom of Greece, or now the Republic of Greece, sponsoring endless terrorist attacks on Turkey. Montefiore: No. But you do have— Frum: And saying that Turkey has no right to exist, and it should all be Greece. Montefiore: No, and that’s one of the huge differences. No one criticizes, no one says it’s disgusting. What, you know—what is Turkish nationalism? Why should the Turks have nationalism? You know, it’s only Israeli nationalism that is constantly challenged. So, but that’s part of it. And the other country that’s very similar—but none of these countries are the same, but there are strong parallels—and the other one is, of course, the creation of Pakistan. Which has huge similarities, and is almost simultaneous with the creation of Israel in 1947. The difference between all three of these, one major difference, is how small the war was in 1948—the Nakba War, or the War of Independence, the War of Israeli Independence was. In Pakistan and India, the loss of life and the scale of deportation and displacement was just colossal. Obviously, India is huge, and there were 1 to 3 million people killed in that process. There were 12 to 14 million people displaced. And out of it came Pakistan—which, again, is an ethno-religious creation which had never existed before, ever, in history, as a result of a new nationalism. And out of it comes, again, not a democracy, but a new sort of nationalism with religious characteristics, a strong military ethos, and huge swaths of population. So the creation of Israel isn’t completely unique, is what I’m saying. Frum: Well, there’s one difference between the creation of Turkey, the creation of Pakistan, and the creation of Israel—that the creation of Israel is the one example that involves a uniquely despised people in the region. The product of exile from other regions, actually now turning out to be quite a successful state. So there’s not just all the things you describe—all the carnage, all the movements of population—but there’s an element of humiliation that is ineradicable. These are the people who are supposed to be absolutely at the bottom of the regional hierarchy. Montefiore: The other half of the parallel would be to the Armenians. But what was different with the Armenians was, the Armenians were much smaller number. Such was the genocide against them that they didn’t recover enough ever to gather the strength to create the states that they were promised. While the Jews did recover from the Holocaust, which they endured, and they did manage to create a state. So there are fascinating parallels here, which I know we don’t have time to go into in detail. But this is so interesting to talk about this. Frum: I want to touch on one last thing. Which is in this discussion, we have used the words genocide over and over again, and we’ve used them to describe very large-scale killing involving the elimination or near-elimination, and followed by expulsion of large numbers of people. Organized according to ideological programs, with a view of elimination. And they are practiced by the Ottomans; they are practiced by the Turkish successors to the Ottomans; they are practiced by the Arab-states successors to the Ottomans, especially Iraq. The genocide that everyone talks about, imagines they know about, is the war between Israel and Hamas in Gaza. That did not involve this scale of killing; that did not involve any kinds of expulsions and that leaves Gaza physically damaged, but its people still alive and in place. And maybe it’s just a gap in what we know. We don’t like to read history. It’s about old people. We don’t like to read about other countries. They don’t speak English. It involves books and not short-form videos. So there’s a lot about this that is off-putting to the modern consumer. But there is something strange about the willingness to remember, to imagine one genocide that didn’t happen and to forget all the genocides that did Montefiore: That’s right. When I think of the word genocide I think that, as a historian, my duty is not to forget the millions of people killed in these successive genocides in the Middle East that I cover in The Cauldron. And this really starts with the million Armenians. But it goes on all the way through—and we’ve touched on some of those stories—the Maronite Christians, the Pontic Greeks, the Ionian Greeks, and all the way through to the Yazidis under the ISIS terror in our very recent history. Saddam Hussein’s killing of the Kurds and using of poison gas to try and exterminate the Kurds. So I think we have an absolute duty to honor these people, and any degradation of the term genocide , which is a special word morally, historically, and legally—anything that degrades the experience of those people is an insult to the memory of these people who must be remembered. And it is our duty to remember them. And nowadays, I think the word has been so degraded; it’s just become a hyperbolic, ideological insult that has become meaningless and is used as much to describe a brutal war in Gaza as it is to describe the blockade of Cuba, for example. And it’s just become a word that we use to describe a bad war or something we don’t like, and that is an insult to the peoples who faced the real genocides in the Middle East, which are chronicled in this book. Frum: Well, it could be a little more sinister than that. Because if your national program, if your ideological program, requires the forgetting of what was done to the Armenians, to the Assyrians, to the Kurds—if that has to be obliterated—then you want to devalue the word. And a great way to devalue a word is to apply it to things that didn’t happen. And that not only indicts the people you want to indict, in this case the Israelis, but it absolves the people who implicitly want to be absolved. And it buries a memory that many people want buried. Frum: Simon, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. Montefiore: Thank you so much for having me, David. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Simon Sebag Montefiore for joining me today for that fascinating discussion. As mentioned at the top of the program, my book this week is The Hidden Hand , by Warren Kinsella, [subtitled] The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda , just published. Warren Kinsella is a prominent Canadian journalist, active for many years in Canadian party politics. He’s a close associate of former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien. He has become passionately involved in recent years in Canada in the debate over the state of Israel and its detractors. Kinsella is very much a shoe-leather journalist. He’s not interested in big theories. He’s interested in getting to the bottom of stories. And The Hidden Hand is his attempt to take his microphone place by place and understand how is it that you have seen this extraordinary surge of anti-Semitic propaganda on the new social media. His big thesis is that this surge is not an organic phenomenon. It’s not that thousands and hundreds of thousands and millions of separate people all over the planet have spontaneously and individually decided to turn their social-media feeds into attacks on the state of Israel. But rather that something is happening here driven by political actors, many of them foreign, but even more worryingly, driven by the nature of social media itself. The algorithm here is taking on a kind of mind of its own, and we are all becoming the algorithm’s captives, and our brain functions are becoming its product. We are moving into a world—and this is a theme I’ve often stressed in these book talks—that is less committed to the word and more to the image. Less committed to rational thought; more committed to emotional action, to emotional response. And therefore more susceptible to manipulation, both by people who want to manipulate and by machines that exist simply to cultivate engagement and to get people to feel anger and upset as a way to maximize engagement. We are building a political culture that is anti-rational, and anti-rational cultures are cultures that are very prone to conspiracy theories, which function as a kind of pseudo-rationality. They seem to explain the world even though they really don’t. And when you become connected to conspiracy theories, at the bottom of all conspiracy theories is the master conspiracy theory about the Jews. The Jews form an important part of the consciousness of ancient myths of Christianity, the killers of Christ; ancient myths of Islam, to deny that the people in the Bible were actually Muslims all along, and the Jews then falsely claim that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and so on were Jews when they were in fact Muslims all along, and so the Jews are falsifiers of their own scripture. And Jews also play an important part in the conspiracy theories of the third great Western religion, Marxism, where Jews are the people who are the ultimate expressions of the false consciousness: the attempt to hold onto religious and national identity instead of the true identity that Marxism wishes us all to embrace, the identity of class. As the target of all three of these kinds of conspiracy theories—in a time when conspiracy theories are emancipated and run wild—well, naturally the Jews occupy an enormous part in the consciousness of the conspirator. And in the images that you see on social media formed to buy and to win appeal, win audience from people prone to conspiracy theories. That’s Kinsella’s story. It’s a very disturbing one, and I recommend the book to people who want to understand what is happening and begin the work of understanding why and what to do about it. That’s it for this week’s David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching or listening. Hope to see you again next week. Remember, the best way to support this program and all of us at The Atlantic is by subscribing to The Atlantic. I hope you will consider doing that. Share, like, and subscribe to this show on whatever platform you use. See you next week. Bye-bye. [ Music ]

items.title: Le Tchad présente à la Banque mondiale ses exigences pour réussir la transformation numérique
items.description: © (DR) Le ministre des Télécommunications, Haliki Choua Mahamat et le représentant de la Banque mondiale au Tchad, Farouk Mollah Banna ont eu des échanges relatif au Projet d’Appui à la transformation numérique et aux perspectives de partenariat. Un aperçu des réalisations faites au Tchad par la Banque Mondiale à travers des projets dans le le secteur des Télécommunications a été fait. Le ministre tchadien a relevé certaines insuffisances dans la mise en œuvre du Projet d’Appui à la transformation du Tchad (PATN). Il en ressort que, 500 sites devront être réalisés dans le cadre dudit projet. Haliki Choua Mahamat souhaite que ces installations techniques soient déployées dans les zones blanches (zone hors réseau) afin de permettre une connectivité. Il évoque également le fait que, le maillage sur le territoire national n’est pas complet. « Six provinces ne sont pas encore connectées par fibre optique » et qu’il faudra encore 8000 Km fibre optique pour un maillage total. Le ministre des Télécommunications déclare que : « sans connectivité totale, on ne pourra atteindre les objectifs de digitalisation et de transformation numérique. » Le membre du gouvernement a également fait un plaidoyer en faveur du Programme régional d’intégration numérique de l’Afrique centrale. Un plaidoyer orienté dans le cadre de l’appui institutionnel et la disposition des experts qualifiés au profit du ministère pour la réalisation des études et des cadres juridiques. Il a également sollicité l’appui de la Banque Mondiale pour la dotation en laboratoires modernes en intelligence artificielle à l’Ecole nationale supérieure des technologies de la Communication (ENASTIC), de l’Université de N’Djamena. Le ministère en charge des Télécommunications estime que, la Banque mondiale, par son représentant apprécie les échanges. Farouk Mollah Banna a : « a éclairé l’assistance ainsi que le Ministre sur les actions éligibles au niveau des portefeuilles de son institution et rassurant de la disponibilité de la Banque Mondiale à appuyer le Tchad dans sa transformation numérique. » L’article Le Tchad présente à la Banque mondiale ses exigences pour réussir la transformation numérique est apparu en premier sur Journal du Tchad .

Etats-Unis: le Congrès américain accentue la pression pour mettre fin à la guerre contre l’Iran
items.description: ETATS-UNIS-IRAN-GUERRE-CONGRES-PRESSION Etats-Unis: le Congrès américain accentue la pression pour mettre fin à la guerre contre l’Iran Ouagadougou, 16 sept. 2026 (AIB)- la Chambre américaine des représentants a adopté, mardi 15 septembre 2026, par 220 voix contre 204, une résolution demandant au président Donald Trump de retirer les forces américaines des opérations militaires contre l’Iran non autorisées par le Congrès. Le texte, adopté pour la troisième fois par la Chambre depuis le début du conflit, a recueilli les voix de l’ensemble des démocrates présents et de sept républicains. Lors des deux précédents votes à la Chambre, seuls quatre élus républicains avaient soutenu une initiative similaire. La résolution s’appuie sur le « War Powers Act », une loi adoptée après la guerre du Vietnam pour encadrer le recours du président aux forces armées et rappeler le rôle du Congrès dans l’autorisation des opérations militaires prolongées. La Chambre avait déjà adopté des résolutions similaires en juin puis en juillet 2026. Au Sénat, une résolution visant à mettre fin à la guerre avait également été approuvée, mais n’avait pas pu aboutir, faute de soutien suffisant des sénateurs républicains. Le coût de la guerre dépasse désormais 38 milliards de dollars, selon le Congressional Budget Office (CBO), qui estime les dépenses supplémentaires à environ trois milliards de dollars par mois en cas de poursuite des opérations. Parallèlement au vote de la Chambre, le représentant républicain Thomas Massie a déposé mardi une procédure de mise en accusation contre le secrétaire à la Défense Pete Hegseth, l’accusant d’avoir ordonné des opérations militaires contre l’Iran sans autorisation du Congrès. Le Pentagone a rejeté ces accusations et réaffirmé son soutien au secrétaire à la Défense. La question de la guerre intervient à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat prévues le 3 novembre 2026, qui détermineront notamment le contrôle des deux chambres du Congrès. La poursuite des hostilités pèse aussi sur les prix de l’énergie et l’inflation aux Etats-Unis. Agence d’Information du Burkina Source : RT

items.title: ‘New pathway for the future’: Quantum Valley Pakistan launched in Islamabad
items.description: Quantum Valley Pakistan, a project likened to America’s Silicon Valley, was launched in Islamabad on Wednesday, with Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal as the chief guest. The Planning Ministry described Quantum Valley Pakistan as a project aimed at connecting academia, entrepreneurs, government and investors to turn “knowledge into solutions, startups into scalable ventures and innovation into national impact”. The project aims to create new pathways for Pakistani talent in AI, quantum computing, fintech, agritech, biotechnology, medtech, digital solutions and autonomous technologies, the ministry said. California’s venture capital firm Plug and Play and the Cambridge Innovation Centre collaborated with the government for the project. Addressing the launch ceremony, Iqbal said, “We are actually setting a new pathway for Pakistan’s future”. “Pakistan is ready for innovation takeoff,” he said. He stressed that this was not an ordinary collaboration, adding that the two companies would bring to Pakistan the “best of innovation in the world and the United States”. Describing the collaboration as a “unique opportunity” for Pakistan, Iqbal expressed hope for the growth of the country’s technology sector. He said that the paradigm of national progress had shifted in the 21st century, with “brain power” now being a key requirement for development. The planning minister added that the foundations for growth being established through Quantum Valley would allow Pakistan’s youth to compete with the youth of the world in terms of tech growth and startups. “Today, we stand at an inflection point,” Iqbal said, adding that in the past two years, Pakistan had seen many successes, namely Marka-i-Haq and recent diplomacy efforts in the US-Iran war . “In my lifetime, I had never seen that for an entire week, media from the US to Australia was only mentioning Islamabad,” he said, referring to the Islamabad talks in April. Successes achieved in defence and diplomacy, if not supplemented by a strong economy, can blur over time, Iqbal said. Alluding to Marka-i-Haq , Iqbal said the nation had to rise to the occasion of “ Marka-i-Taraqi ” and aim to build a $1 trillion economy by 2035 under the Uraan Pakistan programme. He further said the economy should grow to $3 trillion by 2047, when the country marks its centenary. Uraan Pakistan is an initiative of the Planning Ministry designed to advance key projects and reforms set out in the 5Es National Economic Transformation Plan. “These goals are ambitious but not impossible,” Iqbal said. Iqbal urged the nation to move away from the status quo and instead opt for a “transformational path”. The ceremony also included the inauguration of the Global Venture Acceleration Programme for local startups, under which they would receive mentorship over 15 weeks, along with a two-week global immersion in Silicon Valley or Boston.

items.title: Nongoa : trois morts et trois disparus après le naufrage d’une pirogue sur le fleuve Makona
items.description: Un drame s’est produit mardi 15 septembre 2026 sur le fleuve Makona, à Nongoa, dans la préfecture de Guéckédou. Une pirogue motorisée transportant 47 passagers a chaviré en pleine traversée, faisant trois morts et trois disparus. Selon le maire de la commune rurale, Tamba Gabriel Bongono, l’accident est survenu en pleine journée de marché hebdomadaire. Alerté vers 15 heures, il s’est rendu sur les lieux avec le sous-préfet. Le conducteur de la pirogue évoque un blocage du cylindre du moteur, qui aurait provoqué l’arrêt brutal de l’embarcation et une panique générale. Dans la confusion, la pirogue a heurté un morceau de bois avant de se renverser. Sur les 47 personnes à bord, 43 ont été repêchées, dont trois décédées : une femme, un enfant d’un an et demi et un militaire, porté disparu avant d’être retrouvé ce mercredi après-midi. Trois passagers restent introuvables. La présence de gilets de sauvetage et l’intervention des pêcheurs traditionnels « Somono » ont permis de sauver de nombreuses vies. « Ce qui nous a beaucoup aidés, c’est qu’il y avait des gilets de sauvetage. Les Somono ont repêché beaucoup de personnes », témoigne le maire. L’élu local a salué la mobilisation des populations ainsi que celle des autorités administratives et militaires. Il interpelle surtout l’État sur la nécessité de sécuriser cette voie stratégique entre la Guinée et la Sierra Leone. « Nous demandons l’aide de l’État pour la construction d’un pont sur cette partie du fleuve. Le bac qui était là depuis 1958 est gâté. Plusieurs fois, nous remontons cette information, mais sans suite », plaide Tamba Gabriel Bongono. En attendant une solution durable, la traversée du fleuve Makona reste fermée. Amara Souza Soumaoro, correspondant régional à N’zérékoré 621-94-17-77 L’article Nongoa : trois morts et trois disparus après le naufrage d’une pirogue sur le fleuve Makona est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: PHF requests AHF to shift Asian Champions Trophy out of India or relocate Pakistan matches
items.description: The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) has formally asked the Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) to move next month’s men’s Asian Champions Trophy out of India or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue, citing the “sensitive bilateral situation” between the two countries. The request effectively rules out Pakistan playing their matches at the tournament’s scheduled venues in Jalandhar and Mohali unless the AHF agrees to the proposed change. PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani, who is also federal secretary of the Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination, confirmed to Dawn on Wednesday that the federation had formally approached the AHF. The development came two days after Wani had told Dawn that Pakistan’s proposed tour to India was subject to government clearance and that the PHF would abide by whatever decision the government took. Sources in the PHF said the latest decision to seek a neutral venue had been taken on the direction of the federal government. In an official statement issued on Wednesday, Wani said the request had been made to ensure a “safe, dignified and conducive environment” for Pakistan’s players and officials. “The Pakistan Hockey Federation has formally requested the Asian Hockey Federation to relocate the Men’s Asian Champions Trophy 2026 tournament or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue,” Wani said in the statement. The PHF chief, however, made it clear that Pakistan remained committed to the tournament and was willing to face India. “Pakistan remains fully committed to participating in the Asian Champions Trophy and international hockey and is ready to play against all FIH member nations, including India,” he said. The PHF president also said the federation hoped the AHF would consider the proposal positively to ensure Pakistan’s full participation in the tournament. The request comes two days after Indian Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said Pakistan would participate in the tournament, prompting the PHF to clarify that no decision had been taken on the team’s visit to India. Mann, according to a Press Trust of India (PTI) report, had said Pakistan would be among the six teams competing in the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from Oct 27 to Nov 5. “There is no problem in multi-national tournaments. Maybe individual series [between India and Pakistan] cannot take place,” Mann said at an event in Mohali when asked about Pakistan’s participation and whether the requisite clearances had been obtained. The tournament is scheduled to feature hosts India, Pakistan, China, Japan, Malaysia and South Korea. Jalandhar is to host the opening ceremony and all league-stage matches from Oct 27 to Nov 2, while the semi-finals and final are scheduled to be played in Mohali on Nov 4 and 5. Pakistan’s proposed match against India is scheduled for Nov 1 in Jalandhar. The PHF’s latest move means that, while Pakistan is seeking to avoid playing its fixtures in India, it is not seeking to withdraw from the competition. The federation has specifically stated that it is prepared to play India and other FIH member nations at a neutral venue. Pakistan had also withdrawn from last year’s Junior World Cup in Tamil Nadu amid heightened tensions between the two countries.

items.title: South Africa pushes back on US visa curbs
items.description: South Africa on Wednesday hit back at new US visa restrictions over its racial equity policies, accusing the Trump administration of distorting its laws and further straining ties between Washington and one of Africa’s most influential powers. The dispute is the latest front in a broader clash over race, trade and diplomacy that has seen Washington cut aid, impose tariffs, expel South Africa’s ambassador and boycott a G20 summit in Johannesburg, all against the unresolved legacy of white minority rule. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the new visa restrictions would target those who promote “race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said Pretoria viewed the move “with concern” and that Washington was echoing narratives promoted by fringe groups opposed to South Africa’s post-apartheid reforms. “We reiterate that healing the divisions of the past and establishing a society based on democratic values, social justice and fundamental human rights is a constitutional imperative,” Lamola said in a statement. The US did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions but warned of further “severe” action. “This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter,” US ambassador to South Africa, Brent Bozell, said. ‘Hypocrisy’ President Donald Trump has criticised South Africa’s land reform and employment equity laws, which were introduced after the end of apartheid to address racial disparities that remain among the world’s widest. Trump has portrayed the measures as discriminatory against Afrikaners, the white minority descended largely from Dutch settlers, a claim Pretoria rejects. In 2025, he berated President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a “ white genocide ” in South Africa. While the US president has broadly cracked down on immigration, his administration has offered refugee status to thousands of white South Africans it says face persecution. Lamola rejected suggestions that the government was targeting any racial group, saying crime remained a national challenge affecting all South Africans. The opposition uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party, led by former president Jacob Zuma, also condemned the visa restrictions, calling them an affront to South Africa’s sovereignty. “The hypocrisy of Washington’s position is breathtaking. It lectures South Africa, while arming Israel amid the reported killing of more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza,” it said in a statement. Despite the tensions, Pretoria and Washington have remained engaged in efforts to thaw relations. “The discussions have highlighted the need for any resolution to consider South Africa’s unique circumstances and to respect its democracy, constitution, sovereignty, and the will of its people,” Lamola said. South Africa is the largest trading partner of the US on the African continent, with more than 500 US businesses and 30,000 US citizens based in the country. South Africa said last month it would offer a “generous” new trade deal to the United States as it seeks to avoid hefty tariffs that threaten job losses on top of a dire unemployment crisis.

items.title: Hadja, Elhadj, mariages religieux, fraude documentaire : Ce que la ministre Djenabou Touré interdit désormais à l’état civil
items.description: Présidant ce mercredi 16 septembre 2026 la Journée internationale de l'identité, la ministre de l'Administration du territoire et de la Décentralisation, Djenabou Touré, n'a pas mâché ses mots. Face aux officiers délégués d'état civil et des maires de Conakry, la patronne du MATD a dressé un diagnostic sans complaisance des dysfonctionnements qui minent le système national d'identification, de la fraude documentaire dans les mairies à la dérive des titres religieux, en passant par la valeur juridique des mariages célébrés dans les mosquées. ​Dans un discours ferme aux allures de mise en garde, la ministre a directement pointé la responsabilité des agents de l'état civil dans l'altération de l'identité nationale et les failles de sécurité du pays. ​Rectification des noms : la fin de l'anarchie ​Djenabou Touré a d'abord rappelé à l'ordre les agents qui s'octroient le droit de modifier unilatéralement les noms et prénoms des citoyens sur les registres. ​« Il n’est pas permis à un officier d’état civil d’ajouter le nom du village sur le prénom d’un citoyen. C’est la justice qui doit rendre une décision, et cet acte doit être simplement transcrit par l’officier délégué. Que les gens évitent d'ajouter des numéros ou des mentions sur leurs noms tant que la justice ne s’est pas prononcée, afin de nous permettre de corriger l’identité sur des bases légales. » ​Vente d'actes aux étrangers et réseaux clandestins dans les mairies ​Abordant le fléau de la fraude documentaire, la ministre a dénoncé avec véhémence les pratiques mafieuses qui gangrènent certaines municipalités et compromettent la sécurité nationale. ​ « Si vous laissez les étrangers obtenir des actes -fussent-ils des extraits numérisés-, c’est vous qui tronquez l’identité des Guinéens. C’est vous qui faites entrer les fossoyeurs de l’économie et des personnes qui n’ont aucun droit à l’identité nationale. C’est votre responsabilité, chers officiers délégués. S'il y a une rupture dans cette chaîne, la décentralisation bascule, la sécurité de l'identité s'effondre et la fraude continue », a-t-elle pointé du doigt. ​Djenabou Touré s'est également attaquée aux réseaux parallèles installés au cœur même des archives communales : ​« Aujourd’hui, la Guinée est considérée comme un pays de transit de l’immigration illégale. Cela doit cesser. La chaîne commence par l’acte de naissance avant d'aboutir à la carte d’identité et au passeport à la police. Pour mettre fin à cela, nous devons dénoncer ces services parallèles opérant dans vos archives pour dupliquer les numéros de registres et d'actes. Retranscrire illégalement des numéros pour créer de fausses identités est un acte criminel et condamnable », a-t-elle martelé. ​Interdiction des mentions « Hadja » et « Elhadj » sur les actes d'état civil ​Sur la question des qualifications religieuses couramment attribuées aux pèlerins de retour de La Mecque, la ministre a tranché net : ces titres n'ont aucune valeur juridique et n'ont rien à faire sur un document officiel. ​ « Il ne revient pas à un officier délégué d’ajouter « Hadja » ou « Elhadj » sur un acte de naissance. En arabe, ces termes signifient tout simplement « étranger ». Quand vous arrivez à la Mecque, on vous appelle ainsi parce qu’on ne peut pas retenir les noms de millions de pèlerins. C’est une réalité linguistique et administrative qu'il faut intégrer », a-t-elle rappelé. ​Mariages religieux : la transcription à la mairie désormais obligatoire ​Enfin, Djenabou Touré a apporté une clarification majeure sur la valeur légale des unions célébrées dans les lieux de culte, notamment les mosquées. ​« Les actes de mariage délivrés dans les mosquées ne sont pas reconnus par la justice comme des actes de mariage. La loi encadre clairement cela aujourd’hui. Après la célébration religieuse, les époux doivent impérativement se rendre à la commune pour faire transcrire leur union. Il n’y a pas besoin de refaire une cérémonie, c’est une simple formalité administrative pour obtenir l’acte civil. Cela sécurise le couple et évitera à la justice les imbroglios successoraux complexes au moment des décès », a-t-elle conseillé. ​Un coup de balai ferme qui témoigne de la volonté du gouvernement de sécuriser définitivement le fichier de l'état civil guinéen.

items.title: Koulpélogo : Plus de 300 enseignants du secondaire mobilisés autour des réformes éducatives
items.description: Koulpélogo : Plus de 300 enseignants du secondaire mobilisés autour des réformes éducatives Ouargaye, 16 sept. 2026 (AIB)- Plus de 300 enseignants des différents lycées et collèges de la province du Koulpélogo prennent part, du 16 au 18 septembre 2026 à Ouargaye, aux journées d’animation pédagogique consacrées à l’appropriation des réformes du système éducatif. La cérémonie d’ouverture a été marquée par la lecture du discours du ministre de l’Enseignement secondaire, de la Formation professionnelle et technique par le Haut-Commissaire du Koulpélogo, Saïdou Ouédraogo. Selon le directeur provincial de l’enseignement secondaire, de la formation professionnelle et technique, Jacobe Segda, ces journées constituent un cadre de réflexion, d’échanges et de partage d’expériences entre enseignants et encadreurs pédagogiques. Les travaux portent notamment sur la formation professionnelle et technique, l’intégration des technologies de l’information et de la communication (TIC), l’initiation aux métiers et les profils métiers. Quatre thèmes seront développés durant les trois jours à travers des exposés et des échanges. Dans son discours, le ministre a souligné la nécessité d’adapter le système éducatif aux mutations économiques et sociales et d’améliorer l’insertion professionnelle des jeunes. « Nous faisons le choix stratégique et assumé d’orienter une majorité d’apprenants vers l’enseignement professionnel et technique », a-t-il déclaré, selon son discours lu par le Haut-Commissaire. Il a également insisté sur l’importance de l’enseignement scientifique et technologique ainsi que sur l’intégration des TIC pour renforcer la continuité pédagogique et la résilience du système éducatif. Le ministre a salué l’engagement des enseignants et rendu hommage aux Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et aux Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) pour leurs sacrifices en faveur de la sécurisation du territoire et de la continuité des activités scolaires. Ces journées devraient permettre aux participants de mieux s’approprier les réformes et de dégager des stratégies pour leur mise en œuvre dans les établissements du Koulpélogo. Agence d'information du Burkina BP/yos

items.title: Gaza : y a-t-il un génocide ? Avec Johann Soufi
items.description: Le débat sur la qualification des crimes commis par l’armée israélienne à Gaza alimente toujours le débat public français : est-ce un génocide ? D’un point de vue juridique, le terme paraît approprié. Le concept de « génocide » est en effet défini comme un ensemble d’actes – meurtres, viols, déplacement de populations… – guidés par l’intention de détruire en tout ou en partie un groupe en fonction de son ethnie, sa nationalité, sa religion ou « sa race ». De nombreuses organisations non gouvernementales (ONG) indépendantes et experts estiment que cette définition s’applique à la situation à Gaza. La persistance des débats sur l’existence d’un génocide à Gaza interroge donc sur les raisons réelles de la contestation de ce terme. Pourquoi le débat autour de la qualification de génocide à Gaza persiste-t-il ? Quels sont les États et ONG en avant-garde du combat juridique pour sa reconnaissance ? Combien de temps la Cour pénale internationale (CPI) prendra-t-elle à rendre un jugement définitif ? Les débats sur la qualification des crimes commis sont-ils propres au conflit à Gaza ? Quelles sont les conséquences de ces crimes sur l’avenir de la population palestinienne ? Autant d'enjeux abordés avec Johann Soufi, avocat spécialisé en droit international pénal. L’article Gaza : y a-t-il un génocide ? Avec Johann Soufi est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: La Fondation Gates veut mettre l’IA au service des plus vulnérables
items.description: La Fondation Gates annonce un investissement d’au moins un milliard de dollars sur les deux prochaines années pour favoriser une intelligence artificielle plus accessible et mieux adaptée aux besoins des populations défavorisées. L’intelligence artificielle est en train de changer d’échelle. Mais avec elle se pose une question centrale : qui bénéficiera réellement de cette révolution technologique ? C’est tout l’enjeu du 10ᵉ rapport annuel « Goalkeepers » de la Fondation Gates, rendu public le 15 septembre 2026. La Fondation y annonce son intention de consacrer au moins un milliard de dollars au cours des deux prochaines années au développement et au déploiement d’outils d’intelligence artificielle destinés à améliorer l’accès à la santé, à l’éducation, à l’agriculture et aux connaissances. La Fondation identifie à cet égard trois priorités : rendre l’IA accessible dans davantage de langues, développer des solutions adaptées aux réalités locales et investir dans les compétences ainsi que dans les infrastructures numériques. Selon le rapport, l’enjeu linguistique est particulièrement révélateur. Plus de 90 % des données ayant servi à entraîner les premiers grands modèles linguistiques provenaient de sources anglophones. De nombreuses communautés restent donc sous-représentées dans les données qui façonnent ces technologies, souligne le rapport. La santé et l’éducation concentreront chacune 40 % de l’enveloppe annoncée. Dans la santé, les financements pourront soutenir l’aide au diagnostic, la décision clinique, les soins maternels et néonatals ainsi que la recherche pharmaceutique. L’éducation bénéficiera notamment d’outils d’apprentissage personnalisé et d’accompagnement des enseignants. L’agriculture recevra 10 % des financements, notamment pour fournir aux petits exploitants des conseils adaptés à leurs cultures, aux sols et aux conditions météorologiques. Les 10 % restants seront consacrés aux infrastructures et données nécessaires à une IA plus inclusive.
